procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jodhpur
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 10.02.2022 of the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jodhpur in DBCRA No. 123 of 2018 and the order dated 07.07.2022 rejecting the application for suspension of sentence.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court was adjudicating a criminal appeal (DBCRA No. 123 of 2018) against conviction. Asharam @ Ashumal filed an application for suspension of sentence, which was rejected on 07.07.2022. The High Court also considered D.B. Criminal Misc. Third Suspension of Sentence Application (Appeal) No. 220/2022 and D.B. Criminal Misc. Application No. 1 of 2021.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached via a special leave petition (Diary No. 33636 of 2022) challenging the High Court order dated 07.07.2022. One of the grounds for appeal was that the High Court appeal could not be heard until the evidence of Ajay Pal Lamba was recorded. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 1156 of 2023).

directions: Request the High Court to take up the appeal for an expeditious hearing, as the respondent – Asharam @ Ashumal has already suffered incarceration for nearly ten years.
The criminal appeal will be decided by the High Court without being influenced by any observations and findings recorded herein.

issue.issue_text: Whether the test for admitting additional evidence at the appellate stage is the impossibility of pronouncing judgment in its absence, or whether it is to prevent a failure of justice.

law.fact_text: The power to admit additional evidence at the appellate stage is governed by Section 391 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
law.finding: The text references and analyzes Section 391 of the Cr.P.C. as the statutory basis for this power.

law.fact_text: The discretion to admit additional evidence under Section 391 is more restricted than the power to do so at the trial stage under Section 311.
law.finding: The court compares the two sections, noting that the appellate court's discretion is 'somewhat more restricted' because a decision has already been pronounced by the trial court.

law.fact_text: The right to a fair hearing is inherent to due process and the ascertainment of truth.
law.finding: The court grounds its reasoning in the fundamental principles of a fair hearing and the judicial quest for truth.

application.fact_text: The Supreme Court explicitly rejected the test that additional evidence can only be admitted if it is impossible for the appellate court to pronounce a judgment in its absence.
application.finding: The text states, 'The touchstone... is not the impossibility or inability to pronounce the judgment in its absence...'

application.fact_text: Instead, the Court established that the correct test is whether there would be a 'failure of justice' without the additional evidence.
application.finding: The text continues the same sentence by stating, '...but whether there would be a failure of justice without such additional evidence.'

application.fact_text: The Court clarified that this power is a discretion that must be exercised with 'caution and care' and not 'lightly' or in a 'routine and liberal manner.'
application.finding: This discretion is only to be used when the appellate court finds 'on good and justifiable grounds' that a failure of justice would otherwise occur.

application.fact_text: The ultimate purpose of allowing such evidence is to prevent injustice, ensure a fair hearing, and ascertain the truth, while balancing these needs against the risk of delaying proceedings and the right to a speedy trial.
application.finding: The court frames the decision as a balancing act between achieving substantive justice and maintaining procedural fairness and efficiency.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the test for admitting additional evidence at the appellate stage is not the impossibility of pronouncing a judgment without it, but rather whether its absence would lead to a failure of justice. The Court emphasized that this is a discretionary power to be used cautiously to ensure a fair hearing and ascertain the truth.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the test for admitting additional evidence at the appellate stage is the impossibility of pronouncing judgment in its absence, or whether it is to prevent a failure of justice.
appellant_arguments: The appellant likely argued that the High Court applied an incorrect and overly restrictive test for admitting additional evidence under Section 391 of the Cr.P.C. The correct standard is not the impossibility of pronouncing a judgment without the evidence, but the broader principle of whether the evidence is necessary to prevent a failure of justice.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (Asharam @ Ashumal) argued in support of the High Court's decision, likely contending that the conditions for admitting additional evidence were not met. The respondent's counsel relied on the trial court's judgment to support the submission that the additional evidence was not necessary.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The discretionary power to take additional evidence in an appeal is to be exercised with caution and care for good and valid reasons to prevent a failure of justice. The test is not the impossibility of pronouncing a judgment without the additional evidence, but whether a failure of justice would occur in its absence.
obiter: The process of ascertaining the truth requires compliance of procedures and rules of evidence.
In a well-designed system, judicial findings of formal legal truth should coincide with substantive truth.
In a criminal trial, the burden of proof to establish the fact, which has to be proven beyond reasonable doubt, is on the prosecution.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The correct legal standard for admitting additional evidence at the appellate stage is not whether it is impossible to pronounce a judgment without it, but rather whether its absence would lead to a failure of justice. The court explicitly rejected the narrower 'impossibility' test in favor of the broader 'failure of justice' test, clarifying that this judicial discretion must be exercised with caution and only for good and justifiable grounds.
legal_tests_applied: The touchstone of when the additional evidence at the appellate stage may be taken on record is not the impossibility or inability to pronounce the judgment in its absence, but whether there would be a failure of justice without such additional evidence.

This discretion is not to be exercised lightly but requires caution and care as it is to be exercised only in cases when the appellate court finds, on good and justifiable grounds, that there would be a failure of justice without the additional evidence being taken on record.
The appellate court must be equally, if not more cautious, of the desire to delay the hearing of the appeal, or the attempt to lead additional evidence to explore a chance of contradictory evidence.
The request for recall should be bonafide and is to be balanced carefully with relevant considerations, including hardship to the witness and delay of the proceedings.

The discretion to allow additional evidence at the appellate stage should not be exercised in a routine and liberal manner, without the court being satisfied that the prayer has imprints of reasonableness and genuineness to at least consider the worth, credibility and acceptability of the material sought to be brought on record.
policy_considerations: The power to take additional evidence in an appeal is to be exercised to prevent injustice and failure of justice, and thus, must be exercised for good and valid reasons necessitating the acceptance of the prayer.
Every criminal case, it is stated, is a voyage of discovery in which the truth is the quest.
The right to fair hearing is inherent to the concept of due process of law and ascertainment of truth.

Balance between the rights of an accused and the interests and rights of an individual victim and the society, without compromising the right of the accused to a fair trial, has been highlighted by this Court.
Right to speedy trial, including speedy disposal of an appeal, is not the exclusive right of an accused, but an obligation of the court towards the society in general, and the victim in particular.
